doc.title: Hank Cicalo interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, April 30, 2022

title: Miking a koto
summary: Hank recalls an unfamiliar Japanese koto session, and how a mic underneath instead of on top cleaned up the sound.

story.theme_name: Banjo, guitar and the rhythm section: instruments and players
story.community_name: Banjo, guitar and the rhythm section's changing role

blocks.x: Well you’ve seen it all, that’s for sure.

Boy, and more. I’ve seen — I thought I saw it all and then something would — somebody would come in with something I never even heard of before. I remember everybody got into this Japanese thing and suddenly I had a date and they would bring in a koto, you know the Japanese string instrument.

You know it’s a big guitar kind of thing. The strings are on the top. And I just looked at it and how am I going to mic this thing? And I put mics, two microphones on top and it just didn’t sound right. I couldn’t get it to where I wanted it. And I said, “Let’s put a microphone” because you know it sits on a stand. “Put a microphone underneath and let’s see what it sounds like. I put a microphone underneath and all the strings sounded separately, like they were supposed to be. I had the mic on top it didn’t sound right. It sounded cluttered. I mean you just have to experiment sometimes because you know that kind of a guitar sitting up on a stand you could put a microphone underneath it and that’s what I did and it cleaned up the sound. So you know, sometimes you can’t take what the artist is telling you. “Here mic it here.” So you mic it there and God it sounds awful.
